title: Choosing a Database
subtitle: Start from the access pattern, not the brand name — a decision table for the storage choices that come up in interviews.
seoTitle: How to Choose a Database in a System Design Interview
description: SQL vs NoSQL vs cache vs search vs object storage — how to pick storage from access patterns, and how to justify the choice in an interview.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: "Which database?" is rarely the interesting question — the access pattern is. Interviewers want to hear *why*, in terms of how the data is read and written. Most designs end up with two or three stores, each doing one job well.

items: **How is it read?** By key? By range (time, score)? By arbitrary filters? By text search? By location?
**How is it written?** Rate, size, and whether writes must be transactional across rows.
**How consistent must it be?** Money and inventory vs likes and feeds.
**How big will it get?** Fits on one machine (a few TB) or needs sharding from day one?
**What's the shape?** Rows with relations, documents, a graph, blobs, time series?

rows: Sharding is manual work at very large scale
Huge write volume, simple key/range access
Design tables around queries; few joins
Eventually consistent; not a source of truth
High latency per object; serve via CDN
Rarely needed — SQL handles 1–2 hops fine
PostGIS, Redis GEO, geohash in any store
It's a pipe, not a query engine
Key-value or SQL for mappings + Redis cache
SQL/NoSQL for posts + Redis for precomputed feeds
Wide-column (messages by conversation + time) + Redis for presence
SQL for orders, inventory and payments + search index for the catalog
Redis GEO for live driver locations + SQL for trips
Object storage + CDN for media, SQL/NoSQL for metadata

items: **"PostgreSQL" is a fine default.** It handles far more than most people assume (millions of rows per table, JSON, full-text basics, PostGIS). Move off it when you can name the limit you're hitting.

**Justify with the access pattern.** "Messages are always read by conversation, newest first, at high write volume — a wide-column store partitioned by `conversationId` and sorted by time fits that exactly."
**Separate the source of truth from derived stores.** Search indexes and caches are rebuilt from the primary database; say how (change data capture, events).
**Name the partition key** whenever you shard, and check it for hot spots: a celebrity's user ID, today's date, a viral post.
**Big blobs never go in the database.** Store them in object storage and keep the URL.
